questions.prompt: Which statement about The Plague is FALSE?

options.text: About one-third of Europe’s population died.
It was ultimately caused by Yersinia pestis.
It was directly transmitted human-to-human with no animal vector.

questions.explanation: False. Fleas on rats spread it; it was not simple person-toperson transmission.

questions.prompt: Anton van Leeuwenhoek called the microorganisms he observed:
questions.explanation: Animalcules.

questions.prompt: Why did Leeuwenhoek’s discovery of bacteria in rotting teeth not immediately lead to the Germ Theory of Disease?
questions.explanation: He observed more bacteria in rotting teeth than healthy teeth but reversed cause and effect - concluding rotting teeth spontaneously generated bacteria, rather than bacteria causing the rot. It took ~200 more years and the work of Pasteur and Koch to establish the Germ Theory.

questions.prompt: The three Domains of Life are:
questions.explanation: Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya.

questions.prompt: Name the four Kingdoms of Domain Eukarya.
questions.explanation: Animalia, Plantae, Fungi, Protista.

questions.prompt: A virus is best described as:

options.text: An infectious protein with no genetic material
An infectious piece of RNA found only in plants Module 2: Introduction to Microbiology (Part 2)

questions.explanation: A non-living, obligate intracellular parasite.

questions.prompt: Which statement about beneficial microbial roles is FALSE?

options.text: Bacteria and fungi decompose organic matter.
All microbes in nature are pathogenic.
Yeast ferments sugar to produce bread and alcohol.
Lactobacillus is a beneficial probiotic bacterium.

questions.explanation: False. Most microbes are not pathogenic; many play beneficial roles.

questions.prompt: Pasteur’s swan-necked flask experiment helped disprove:
questions.explanation: Spontaneous generation.

questions.prompt: What two things did Pasteur’s fermentation research show, and how did this connect to the Germ Theory of Disease?
questions.explanation: Pasteur showed yeast causes fermentation and bacteria cause spoilage - establishing that specific living microbes cause specific effects, which laid the conceptual foundation for microbes causing disease (the Germ Theory).

questions.prompt: Alexander Fleming is best known for discovering:
questions.explanation: Penicillin.

questions.prompt: Name the contributions of Semmelweis, Nightingale, and Lister toward combatting disease. Module 3: Prokaryotic Cells (Part 1)
questions.explanation: Semmelweis - hand washing. Nightingale - hospital cleanliness. Lister - germicides.

questions.prompt: Which statement about bacterial shapes/arrangements is FALSE?
questions.explanation: False. Diplo- means pairs/two, not chains (strepto- means chains).

questions.prompt: Flagella are used primarily for:
questions.explanation: Motility.

questions.prompt: Describe the structural difference between a Gram-positive and Gram-negative cell envelope.
questions.explanation: Gram-positive: thick peptidoglycan layer with teichoic/lipoteichoic acids, no outer membrane. Gram-negative: thin peptidoglycan layer plus an outer membrane containing lipopolysaccharide (LPS).

questions.prompt: Penicillin works by:
questions.explanation: Inhibiting peptidoglycan cross-link synthesis.

questions.prompt: What makes Acid-Fast bacteria’s cell walls unique, and why does this matter clinically?
questions.explanation: Acid-Fast walls contain mycolic acid, making them waxy - this resists phagocytosis, repels many antibiotics, and repels standard stains, requiring a special Acid-Fast stain (clinically relevant for organisms like Mycobacterium tuberculosis).

questions.prompt: Which genus of bacteria naturally lacks a cell wall?
questions.explanation: Mycoplasma.

questions.prompt: Which statement about membrane transport is FALSE?

options.text: Facilitated diffusion requires a transport protein.
Active transport moves substances from low to high concentration.
Osmosis is the diffusion of solute.

questions.explanation: False. Osmosis is the diffusion of the solvent (water), not the solute.

questions.prompt: A cell placed in a hypertonic solution will:
questions.explanation: Shrink (plasmolysis).

questions.prompt: Why is the difference between 70S and 80S ribosomes clinically important?
questions.explanation: Bacterial (70S) and human (80S) ribosomes are structurally different, so antibiotics like tetracycline can selectively target bacterial ribosomes without harming the patient’s ribosomes.

questions.prompt: Plasmids are clinically relevant primarily because they:

options.text: Can carry and spread antibioticresistance genes
Are the site of protein synthesis

questions.explanation: Can carry and spread antibiotic-resistance genes.

questions.prompt: What are endospores, and why are they clinically significant? Module 5: Metabolism (Part 1)
questions.explanation: Endospores are highly resilient dormant structures formed by some bacteria (Bacillus, Clostridium, Clostridioides) under stress; they resist heat, drying, and disinfectants, letting bacteria survive harsh conditions and later germinate back into active, diseasecausing cells.

questions.prompt: Which statement about catabolism and anabolism is FALSE?
questions.explanation: False. Anabolism is endergonic (requires energy), not exergonic.

questions.prompt: ATP stores energy in:

options.text: The bond holding its third phosphate

questions.explanation: The bond holding its third phosphate.

questions.prompt: What is activation energy, and how do enzymes affect it?
questions.explanation: Activation energy is the energy required to initiate a reaction. Enzymes lower the activation energy needed, speeding up the reaction.

questions.prompt: A competitive inhibitor works by:

options.text: Binding the active site and blocking substrate
Adding a phosphate group to the enzyme

questions.explanation: Binding the active site and blocking substrate.

questions.prompt: Explain why sulfa drugs are safe for human use even though they block folic acid synthesis. Module 6: Metabolism (Part 2)
questions.explanation: Humans/animals obtain folic acid from their diet rather than synthesizing it via the enzyme sulfa drugs block; bacteria must synthesize their own folic acid, so the drug selectively harms bacteria without affecting the host’s folic acid supply.

questions.prompt: Which statement about aerobic respiration is FALSE?

options.text: The electron transport chain produces the majority of the ATP.

questions.explanation: False. Glycolysis alone only produces 2 ATP; the majority (34) comes from the electron transport chain.

questions.prompt: The final electron acceptor in aerobic respiration is:
questions.explanation: Oxygen.

questions.prompt: Compare aerobic respiration and fermentation in terms of ATP yield and oxygen requirement.
questions.explanation: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and yields 38 ATP total (via all four stages). Fermentation uses no oxygen, only completes glycolysis, and yields just 2 ATP.

questions.prompt: Alcoholic fermentation, performed by yeast, produces:
questions.explanation: Ethanol and CO2.

questions.prompt: What are oxidation and reduction, and how do they relate to glucose breakdown? Module 7: Microbial Growth
questions.explanation: Oxidation = losing electrons; reduction = gaining electrons. Glucose is progressively oxidized as it’s broken down, and its electrons are transferred to electron carriers (NAD+ -> NADH, FAD -> FADH2), which become reduced.

questions.prompt: Which statement about pure vs. mixed cultures is FALSE?

options.text: A pure culture comes from a single cell.
A mixed culture has multiple species.
Streak plating helps isolate pure cultures.
Agar solidifies growth media without melting at body temperature.

questions.explanation: False. Robert Koch (not Fannie Hesse) pioneered pure culturing; Fannie Hesse contributed the idea of using agar.

questions.prompt: Which oxygen category describes Clostridium botulinum?
questions.explanation: Obligate anaerobe.

questions.prompt: Which temperature and pH categories include most human pathogens, and why?
questions.explanation: Mesophiles (temperature) and Neutrophiles (pH), because human body temperature (~37°C) and pH (~7.35) fall within those respective ranges.

questions.prompt: Helicobacter pylori survives stomach acid by:

options.text: Producing urease to create a local microenvironment

questions.explanation: Producing urease to create a local microenvironment.

questions.prompt: Describe the four phases of a bacterial growth curve in order.
questions.explanation: Lag phase (slow growth) -> Log/exponential phase (rapid doubling) -> Stationary phase (division rate = death rate, population levels off) -> Death phase (death rate exceeds division rate).

questions.prompt: A culture starts with 1,000 cells and has a 20minute generation time. How many cells are present after 1 hour? Module 8: Control of Microbial Growth
questions.explanation: 60 minutes / 20-minute generation time = 3 doublings. 2^3 = 8. 1,000 x 8 = 8,000 cells.

questions.prompt: Which statement about sterilization/disinfection is FALSE?

options.text: Sterilization destroys all microbes including endospores.
Disinfection destroys most, but not necessarily all, microbes.
Antiseptics are safe for use on living tissue.
Boiling for 10 minutes achieves full sterilization.

questions.explanation: False. Boiling does not destroy endospores, so it disinfects but does not achieve full sterilization.

questions.prompt: Which of these medical item categories requires the item to be sterile because it penetrates tissue?
questions.explanation: Critical.

questions.prompt: Why are Bacillus, Clostridium, and Clostridioides difficult to control?
questions.explanation: They form endospores, which resist heat, drying, and many chemical disinfectants, letting them survive treatments that kill ordinary vegetative bacterial cells.

questions.prompt: An autoclave achieves sterilization at:
questions.explanation: 121°C at 15 PSI for 15 minutes.

questions.prompt: Compare how heat and radiation each control microbial growth at the molecular level.
questions.explanation: Heat controls microbes by denaturing proteins (destroying their functional shape). Radiation controls microbes by mutating their DNA (damaging genetic material so they can’t replicate/function).

questions.prompt: Which germicide category is a pressurized gas capable of killing endospores?
questions.explanation: Ethylene oxide.

questions.prompt: Which pairing of scientist to contribution is FALSE?

options.text: Robert Koch — proved the Germ Theory of Disease.
Louis Pasteur — proposed microbes cause disease.
Robert Hooke — discovered bacteria using a microscope.
Hans Christian Gram — developed the Gram stain.

questions.explanation: False. Anton van Leeuwenhoek (not Robert Hooke) is credited with first observing bacteria; Hooke coined the term “cell” and pioneered microscopy more generally.

questions.prompt: Which structure allows bacteria to exchange antibiotic-resistance genes via conjugation?
questions.explanation: Sex pilus (conjugation pilus).

questions.prompt: Explain the relationship between a bacterium’s capsule and biofilm formation, with an example.
questions.explanation: A capsule (glycocalyx), made of carbohydrate, allows bacteria to adhere to surfaces and each other, enabling biofilm formation e.g., Streptococcus mutans forms a biofilm on teeth, causing cavities.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an example of a facultative anaerobe used throughout this course as a common model organism?
questions.explanation: Escherichia coli.

questions.prompt: Name the two components of peptidoglycan and explain why the amino acid cross-links matter.
questions.explanation: NAG (N-acetylglucosamine) and NAM (N-acetylmuramic acid). The amino acid cross-links between these sugar strands give the cell wall its rigidity and strength, letting it resist osmotic pressure that would otherwise rupture the cell.

questions.prompt: Which statement about enzyme regulation is FALSE?

options.text: Feedback inhibition involves a pathway’s product inhibiting an earlier enzyme.
The allosteric site is the same as the active site.
Phosphorylation can activate an inactive enzyme.
Noncompetitive inhibitors bind the allosteric site.
Competitive inhibitors resemble the natural substrate.

questions.explanation: False. The allosteric site is separate from (not the same as) the active site.

questions.prompt: Which disease is caused by Streptococcus pyogenes?
questions.explanation: Strep throat.

questions.prompt: Describe how Clostridioides difficile causes diarrhea, from ingestion to infection.
questions.explanation: C. difficile spores and vegetative cells are ingested; stomach acid kills the vegetative cells, but spores survive and germinate in the small intestine; the bacteria then multiply and cause infection (diarrhea) in the large intestine.

questions.prompt: Which molecule is the final electron acceptor for some bacteria that do NOT use oxygen, producing H2S?
questions.explanation: Sulfur.

questions.prompt: Why is the Golden Age of Microbiology (mid-1800s to early 1900s) significant, and what four questions did scientists explore during it?
questions.explanation: It was a ~50-year period (mid-1800s to early 1900s) when scientists resolved four major questions: Does life arise spontaneously? What causes fermentation? What causes disease? How can disease be prevented/treated? - work that established modern microbiology’s foundations.

questions.prompt: Tetracycline is able to selectively target bacteria because it acts on:
questions.explanation: The 70S ribosome.

questions.prompt: Compare Gram-positive, Gram-negative, and AcidFast cell envelopes in terms of peptidoglycan thickness and any additional distinguishing component.
questions.explanation: Gram-positive: thick peptidoglycan, no outer membrane, plus teichoic/lipoteichoic acids. Gram-negative: thin peptidoglycan, plus an outer membrane with lipopolysaccharide (LPS). Acid-Fast: peptidoglycan layer similar to Gram-positive (no outer membrane), but studded with waxy mycolic acid.
